The '''Great Elephant Census''' was an Africa-wide census designed to provide accurate data about the number and distribution of [[African elephant]]s by using standardized aerial surveys of terrain in Africa.<ref name=NG>{{cite web |url=http://news.nationalgeographic.com/2016/08/wildlife-african-elephants-population-decrease-great-elephant-census/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160831183926/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/2016/08/wildlife-african-elephants-population-decrease-great-elephant-census/ |archive-date=31 August 2016 |title=African Elephant Numbers Plummet 30 Percent, Landmark Survey Finds |author=Paul Steyn |date=31 August 2016 |access-date=1 September 2016 |work=National Geographic}}</ref> The census was published on the online journal ''[[PeerJ]]'' on 31 August 2016<ref>{{cite journal|title=Continent-wide survey reveals massive decline in African savannah elephants|date=31 August 2016|journal=PeerJ|doi=10.7717/peerj.2354 |last1=Chase |first1=Michael J. |last2=Schlossberg |first2=Scott |last3=Griffin |first3=Curtice R. |last4=Bouché |first4=Philippe J.C. |last5=Djene |first5=Sintayehu W. |last6=Elkan |first6=Paul W. |last7=Ferreira |first7=Sam |last8=Grossman |first8=Falk |last9=Kohi |first9=Edward Mtarima |last10=Landen |first10=Kelly |last11=Omondi |first11=Patrick |last12=Peltier |first12=Alexis |last13=Selier |first13=S.A. Jeanetta |last14=Sutcliffe |first14=Robert |volume=4 |article-number=e2354 |pmid=27635327 |pmc=5012305 |doi-access=free }}</ref> at a cost of US$7&nbsp;million.<ref name="NPR">{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2016/08/31/492124724/african-elephant-population-declines-by-30-percent|title=African Elephant Population Declines By 30 Percent|author=Rebecca Hersher|date=31 August 2016|access-date=1 September 2016|publisher=The Two-way}}</ref> It's considered the largest wildlife census in history.

==History==
The scientific community believes that there were as many as 20 million African elephants in the 1800s and at the time of the [[Scramble for Africa]]. By 1979, an estimated 600,000 elephants remained on the continent, around a 97% decrease from pre-colonization populations.<ref name=NG />

At the time, a pan-African elephant census had not been conducted since around 1979. The idea of a modern census was devised by the group Elephants Without Borders and supported, both financially and logistically, by [[Paul Allen]]. It was also supported by other organizations and individuals, including African Parks, the [[Frankfurt Zoological Society]], [[Wildlife Conservation Society]], [[The Nature Conservancy]], [[IUCN|IUCN African Elephant Specialist Group]], Howard Frederick, Mike Norton-Griffith, Kevin Dunham, Chris Touless, and Curtice Griffin (as credited by the final report).<ref name=Census>{{cite web|url=http://www.greatelephantcensus.com/the-census/|title=Great Elephant Census – The Census|access-date=1 September 2016|year=2016|publisher=[[Vulcan Inc.|Vulcan]]}}</ref>

Mike Chase, the founder of Elephants Without Borders, was the lead scientist of the census. Chase led a group of 90 scientists and 286 crew members in 18 African countries for over two years to collect the data. During this time the team flew a distance of over {{convert|500000|km|mi|0}}, equivalent to flying to the moon and a quarter of the way back, in over 10,000 hours of collecting data.<ref name=NG /> The area covered represents 93% of the elephants known range.<ref name=NG />

[[Forest Elephant]]s which live in central and western Africa were excluded from the survey.<ref name=NG />

==Report==
[[File:Elephant576.JPG|thumb|An elephant skull with removed tusks, indicating that it was killed by poachers, [[Voi]] area, Kenya]]
The final report was released on 31 August 2016 in Honolulu at the IUCN World Conservation Congress. Data collected showed a 30 percent decline in the population of African savanna elephant in 15 of the 18 countries surveyed.<ref name=CFR>{{cite web|url=http://www.greatelephantcensus.com/blog/2016/8/31/press-release-great-elephant-census-final-results|title=Great Elephant Census Final Results|date=31 August 2016|publisher=Vulcan}}</ref> The reduction occurred between 2007 and 2014, representing a loss of approximately 144,000 elephants.<ref name=NG/>

The total population of Africa's savannah elephants were enumerated as 352,271, far lower than what the surveyors had previously estimated.<ref name=NG />

Three countries with significant elephant populations were not surveyed; [[Namibia]] didn't release any figures and both [[South Sudan]] and the [[Central African Republic]] were in the middle of an armed conflict.<ref name=Guardian>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2016/aug/31/poaching-drives-huge-30-decline-in-africas-savannah-elephants|title=Poaching drives huge 30% decline in Africa's savannah elephants|date=1 September 2016|access-date=1 September 2016|newspaper=The Guardian}}</ref>

The rate of decline in the population is also accelerating and reached 8% in 2014.<ref name=Huff>{{cite web|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com.au/entry/elephant-census-poaching_us_57c7573be4b0e60d31dd1580|title=A New Elephant Census Shows The Devastating Impact Of Poaching|date=1 September 2016|access-date=1 September 2016|work=The Huffington Post}}</ref> The loss of population is primarily a result of [[poaching]] with the elephants being killed for their [[tusk]]s. The [[ivory]] is then illegally sold around the world, such as [[China]] and [[United States|the United States]]. As a result of the survey, it was estimated that approximately 100 elephants were killed every day for ivory. Losses of the elephant's [[habitat]] are another reason for the drastic reduction in population.<ref name=Huff/>

84% of the population were sighted in legally protected areas, such as reserves and national parks. Not only that, a high number of carcasses were found in the same protected areas, indicating poaching.<ref name=CFR/>
